units.filledPassage:
A neighbourhood time bank allowed members to provide approved services and earn credits measured in hours. The arrangement encouraged reciprocity, a pattern of mutual giving and receiving, without requiring the person who received one service to repay the same provider directly. It was distinct from an ordinary cash wage for employment: the scheme's credits did not claim to settle every legal question about work.

When a member completed an accepted task, the recorded service was a contribution to the scheme. A coordinator checked that both parties agreed the task had occurred. An entry became verified after that confirmation, rather than merely because one participant had submitted a request.

Transactions were kept in a ledger, a chronological accounting record. A member's available balance reflected credits earned and used under the local rules. Recording the same task twice would distort that amount even if the duplicated descriptions were individually plausible.

Using earned credits to receive a service was redemption. The scheme's ability to meet such requests depended on willing members and suitable skills; a positive account did not guarantee immediate access to every kind of assistance. The coordinators therefore distinguished a record from a promise of unlimited supply.

The rules defined eligibility, the conditions under which a person could join and participate. They also specified an expiry date after which unused credits would no longer remain valid. That condition was explained before members joined, rather than introduced after their contributions.

If participants disagreed about a recorded task, a dispute could be submitted for review. The review considered the evidence and the announced rules; it did not assume that the larger recorded balance necessarily belonged to the more truthful person. The seminar used the example to separate social purpose, accounting events and obligations. Calling the arrangement mutual aid did not remove the need to explain what each account entry meant.
